title: Company Picnic

jokes.text: Erin catches herself saying 'when he gets up' and self-corrects to 'gets back'
jokes.setup: Erin is on the phone covering for Michael, using professional receptionist language
jokes.punchline: She nearly blurts out that he's asleep, catches it mid-sentence, but the correction itself reveals the truth
jokes.explanation: This is a beautifully economical piece of character comedy. Erin's self-correction is the joke — the correction itself is the confession. It's a classic slip that reveals character (she's new, trying hard, but not quite seasoned enough to fully cover). The structure is tight and it earns its laugh through Erin's specific voice.

jokes.text: Erin's escalating explanation: 'Michael had chicken pot pie for lunch... an entire chicken pot pie... an entire family-sized chicken pot pie... and then he fell asleep.'
jokes.setup: Erin is explaining to the documentary crew why the office is quiet and everyone is tiptoeing
jokes.punchline: The triple escalation — 'entire,' then 'family-sized,' then the consequence of falling asleep — builds absurdity through deadpan specificity
jokes.explanation: The joke's structure is the joke. Three ascending qualifiers ('entire,' then 'family-sized,' then the nap consequence) work like a triple-beat punchline. It's a great cold open gag because it tells us everything we need to know about Michael's character in one sentence while being genuinely funny. The rhythm of the escalation is particularly well-executed.

jokes.text: Erin checks the clock while saying 'which actually should be in about...' then a long pause and the camera cuts to Michael waking up at [01:16] like clockwork
jokes.setup: Erin says the 5pm alarm will go off in about ten minutes and everyone is frantically changing clocks
jokes.punchline: The long pause implies real-time waiting; Michael then wakes up exactly as predicted, implying the plan worked
jokes.explanation: The real-time waiting gag — the long pause between 'in about...' and the payoff of Michael rising — is a structurally clever sitcom beat. The caption 'like clockwork' makes it explicit. Functional and well-timed but not particularly original.

jokes.text: The entire scheme of changing Michael's computer clock and watch so he wakes up thinking it's 5pm
jokes.setup: The office wants to leave early but Michael is asleep and is technically still the boss
jokes.punchline: Rather than simply leaving or waking him, the employees engage in an elaborate multi-person conspiracy to manipulate all time-keeping devices around a sleeping man
jokes.explanation: The comedy here is in the elaborate absurdity of the solution versus the simplicity of just leaving. It reveals that the employees are simultaneously terrified of and condescending toward Michael — they won't just walk out, but they'll construct an entire theatrical deception instead. Character-rich and conceptually sound.

jokes.text: 'I have an appointment with the horse doctor. How that horse became a doctor, I don't know.'
jokes.setup: Dwight explains he needs to leave and references a horse doctor
jokes.punchline: He deliberately plays on the ambiguity of 'horse doctor' — a doctor for horses vs. a horse who is a doctor — and the delivery implies he momentarily entertained the absurd interpretation
jokes.explanation: This is a standout line. The joke is perfectly structured — 'horse doctor' is the setup, the punchline is him sincerely wondering how a horse became a doctor, then the immediate self-correction to the far darker 'regular doctor who shoots your horse in the head' makes it even better. It's extremely character-specific to Dwight: only he would say this with complete sincerity. Highly quotable. Comparable in quality to the 8.0 anchor — perfectly economical, original within the show's universe, and it couldn't come from anyone but Dwight.

jokes.text: 'I'm kidding. He's just a regular doctor who shoots your horse in the head when its leg is broken.'
jokes.setup: Dwight 'corrects' himself after the horse doctor joke, implying the correction will be more normal
jokes.punchline: The 'correction' is actually darker and more absurd — a doctor whose job is to euthanize horses by shooting them
jokes.explanation: This is the better half of the horse doctor two-parter and arguably the best joke in the cold open. The structure of 'I'm kidding' followed by something MORE disturbing is a classic misdirection. But what makes it exceptional is Dwight's total sincerity — he genuinely thinks this is the clarifying, reassuring correction. The specificity of 'shoots your horse in the head when its leg is broken' is dark, accurate to Dwight's farming worldview, and brilliantly delivered. Earns its high score because it works on multiple levels simultaneously.

jokes.text: Michael wakes up exactly when the manipulated clock hits 5pm — 'Like clockwork' — confirming the plan worked perfectly
jokes.setup: The office has manipulated the clocks to make Michael think it's 5pm
jokes.punchline: He wakes up exactly on cue, validating the absurd plan — and someone offscreen remarks 'like clockwork,' which is literally and ironically true
jokes.explanation: The payoff to the clock-manipulation scheme. 'Like clockwork' is a gentle ironic joke — it's literally about a clock. Works but doesn't transcend the setup.

jokes.text: 'What's so funny?' / 'You had to be there!' / 'Geography joke.'
jokes.setup: Michael wakes up and finds everyone in good spirits as they leave
jokes.punchline: Someone explains the mirth with 'geography joke' — which tells us nothing and is clearly a non-explanation; the joke was apparently at Michael's expense
jokes.explanation: The comedy here is in the uselessness of 'geography joke' as an explanation. It's a deliberately unsatisfying answer that tells us the office is keeping Michael in the dark about the whole scheme. Functional but not particularly layered.

jokes.text: 'Let's all go home. Come on. See you all tamale.'
jokes.setup: Michael dismisses everyone for the day
jokes.punchline: 'See you all tamale' — a malapropism/pun on 'tomorrow' delivered with total confidence by Michael, who clearly thinks it's clever
jokes.explanation: A classic Michael Scott move — the groan-worthy pun delivered with complete self-satisfaction. 'Tamale' for 'tomorrow' is the kind of thing Michael would absolutely do and be proud of. It's not the sharpest joke but the character integration is strong. It's a fitting capper to the cold open.

jokes.text: 'Should I have left the car running?'
jokes.setup: Jim and Pam are steeling themselves to walk into the picnic
jokes.punchline: Jim suggests they should have staged a getaway car — treating a company picnic like a heist or hostage situation
jokes.explanation: Clean, economical, very Jim. The getaway-car framing for a company picnic is an elegant absurdist escalation of his dread. Six words, perfectly timed. Good example of Jim's deadpan at its best.

jokes.text: Pam recalls the drunk guy who grabbed her 'for balance' at last year's picnic; Jim confirms: 'You don't grab these for balance.'
jokes.setup: Jim and Pam discuss bad memories of last year's picnic; Pam mentions a drunk guy who grabbed her claiming it was for balance
jokes.punchline: Jim's deadpan 'you don't grab these for balance' — affirming the excuse was absurd without spelling it out
jokes.explanation: Jim's response is well-delivered and the 'for balance' excuse is an amusing piece of drunk logic. It's a bit of a throwaway gag but executed cleanly. The gesture-implied visual element (Pam's presumably physical assets being referenced without being named) adds a layer.

jokes.text: Dwight and his friend debating SPF levels; Dwight reveals his homemade SPF/insect repellant combination and asks 'You think the EPA would ever allow that much DEET?'
jokes.setup: Two people are comparing sunscreen numbers at the picnic
jokes.punchline: Dwight has created his own illegal-grade combination sunscreen/insect repellant that exceeds EPA-permitted DEET levels
jokes.explanation: This is pure Dwight — the self-sufficiency, the survivalist paranoia, the gleeful disregard for regulatory safety limits. The EPA line is the kicker and it works because Dwight's pride is palpable. Only Dwight would formulate his own DEET cocktail and be smug about it.

jokes.text: Dwight's confessional about Rolph: 'We met in a shoe store. I heard him asking for a shoe that could increase his speed and not leave any tracks.'
jokes.setup: Dwight introduces his best friend Rolph to the documentary crew
jokes.punchline: The criteria Rolph used to shop for shoes — increasing speed while leaving no tracks — strongly imply sinister or at minimum extremely paranoid intentions, but Dwight finds this a perfectly reasonable basis for friendship
jokes.explanation: This is the strongest line in the episode and one of the best Dwight jokes in the series. The craft is exceptional: the shoe store is such a mundane, civilian setting that Rolph's requirement — shoes that increase speed AND leave no tracks — is maximally sinister by contrast. The joke works on multiple levels: it reveals both Rolph's terrifying nature AND Dwight's, because Dwight heard this criteria and thought 'yes, this is my people.' The economy is perfect; every word is load-bearing. Highly quotable, original, and absolutely could not come from any other character. Comparable to or slightly above the 8.0 anchor example.

jokes.text: Michael spots Holly with her boyfriend AJ and says 'We're just friends.' Then, upon seeing AJ: 'Wait a second. Who let you in here is what I wanna know.'
jokes.setup: Michael sees Holly, who has a new boyfriend. He has clearly been pining for her.
jokes.punchline: Michael first denies any feelings ('we're just friends'), then immediately and jealously challenges AJ's right to be at a public company picnic
jokes.explanation: Michael's transparent jealousy is classic character comedy. The 'who let you in here' line at a company picnic — an event presumably anyone affiliated with Dunder Mifflin can attend — reveals his petty territorial feelings hilariously. The juxtaposition of 'we're just friends' with immediate hostility is well-structured.

jokes.text: 'I see they're letting just anybody in here.' (Michael to Holly, implying AJ specifically)
jokes.setup: Michael is trying to be cool about Holly having a boyfriend while clearly being bothered
jokes.punchline: He delivers a transparent passive-aggressive dig at AJ disguised as a casual observation
jokes.explanation: This is the second beat of Michael's jealousy riff. It's slightly weaker than the first — the 'letting just anybody in' line is more of a filler passive-aggressive comment than a real joke. Functional cringe but not particularly original.

jokes.text: When Holly introduces AJ as her boyfriend, Michael says: 'A little bit. I meet a lot of people.'
jokes.setup: Holly introduces AJ as 'my boyfriend' and presumably asks if Michael remembers him
jokes.punchline: Michael's dismissive 'a little bit. I meet a lot of people' — implying AJ is unmemorable while also being transparently rude — is delivered as if it's perfectly normal small talk
jokes.explanation: This is a great Michael line. The pretense that he barely remembers the man dating the woman he loves, executed with total sincerity, is peak Michael Scott social awkwardness. 'I meet a lot of people' as a cover for jealousy is both a good joke and genuinely revealing of his character — it's the kind of thing you might actually say if you were desperately trying to seem unbothered.

jokes.text: Michael offering lemonade: 'Or one of you? Or both of you. Either or. The combinations are endless.'
jokes.setup: Michael awkwardly offers lemonade to Holly and AJ while clearly flustered by their presence
jokes.punchline: His math on lemonade distribution spirals into 'the combinations are endless' — an absurd non-statement about two people and a drink
jokes.explanation: Beautifully observed cringe comedy. Michael's social brain short-circuits trying to process Holly-plus-boyfriend as a unit, and it manifests in an over-analysis of a simple drink offer. 'The combinations are endless' for two people and one beverage is a perfectly absurd conclusion. It's very specifically Michael's voice — the rambling, the false profundity. Strong joke.

jokes.text: AJ asks for iced tea; Michael says 'You can go to hell.' Then immediately: 'I'm kidding!'
jokes.setup: Michael has offered beverages and AJ requests iced tea instead of lemonade
jokes.punchline: Michael's utter contempt for AJ surfaces as a blunt 'you can go to hell' before he catches himself
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The setup is completely mundane — someone asking for a drink — and the punchline is maximally disproportionate. The fact that it comes in response to iced tea is what makes it so funny; AJ didn't do anything remotely offensive. The rapid backpedal ('I'm kidding!') and then his extravagant promise to bring 'the best iced tea in the world' to cover his ass makes the sequence even richer. Pure Michael Scott: the jealousy leaks out despite his best efforts.

jokes.text: Michael's confessional: 'I lied to Kevin. Holly and I can never be just friends.' Then reveals his list, starting with 'You and I are soup snakes.'
jokes.setup: Michael told Kevin (off-screen) that he and Holly are 'just friends.' He's now in a confessional about his real feelings, listing reasons they should be together.
jokes.punchline: His bullet-pointed list of romantic arguments begins with 'You and I are soup snakes' — a non-sequitur that is meaningless and clearly not a reason for romance
jokes.explanation: This is a classic Michael Scott moment. The joke has two layers: (1) Michael has written a formal bullet-point list for something as organic as love, which is absurdly bureaucratic, and (2) the first item on the list is 'soup snakes' — clearly a mangled version of 'soul mates' that he doesn't realize is wrong. What makes it exceptional is that Michael himself doesn't know why he wrote it. His genuine confusion mid-confessional ('and the reason is... because in terms of the soup, we like to...') before correcting to 'soul mates' is perfectly written. Highly quotable and very character-specific.

jokes.text: 'And the reason is... Because, in terms of the soup, we like to...' — Michael trails off, unable to explain 'soup snakes'
jokes.setup: Michael has written 'soup snakes' as point one and is now asked to elaborate
jokes.punchline: He cannot finish the sentence. The joke is the silence — Michael discovers live that he doesn't know what he meant
jokes.explanation: The follow-through on 'soup snakes' — Michael's genuine real-time confusion as he tries to explain his own metaphor. The incomplete sentence IS the punchline. Together with joke 19 this forms one of the best two-beat jokes in the episode. The silence and trailing off characterizes Michael's tendency to make grand gestures on empty foundations.

jokes.text: Jim's confessional: 'Must be nice to get a rest from all your rest.' (about Charles)
jokes.setup: Charles (Jim's new boss) is apparently relaxing at the picnic; Jim is commenting in confessional
jokes.punchline: 'Must be nice to get a rest from all your rest' — implying Charles does nothing
jokes.explanation: A decent dig but feels slightly petty rather than sharp. The wordplay on 'rest from your rest' is the best part — the repetition creates an elegant economy. Competent Jim snark but not his best.

jokes.text: Pam offers to beat up Charles; Jim says: 'I shouldn't have to ask you to do that. You should just do it.'
jokes.setup: Pam offers to handle Jim's beef with Charles by beating him up
jokes.punchline: Jim's response suggests he's disappointed she asked rather than taking initiative — treating 'beat up my boss' as an obvious, proactive thing a good partner would do unprompted
jokes.explanation: Good relationship comedy. Jim framing violence as a duty-of-care in a committed relationship — something Pam should just know to do — applies the logic of relationship advice columns to absurd ends. It's well-structured and gets a solid laugh. Their chemistry sells it.

jokes.text: Dwight's lineup for the volleyball game and his invocation of 'the humiliation we suffered last year' at softball due to Jim's 'spider-in-the-mitt incident'
jokes.setup: Dwight is running a pre-game pep talk and cites historical grievances to motivate the team
jokes.punchline: The spider-in-the-mitt incident is referenced seriously as a defining trauma; Jim dryly notes 'I could have died'
jokes.explanation: The callback to a fictional spider-in-mitt incident is treated with Dwight-appropriate seriousness, and Jim's deadpan 'I could have died' as a defense rather than a joke lands well. Competent character comedy but not peak material.

jokes.text: Ryan asks Dwight to put Erin on his row ('Bro-migo'); Dwight misreads it as Ryan wanting Erin to set him up for spikes, and offers Phyllis instead: 'She's the best setter on the team.'
jokes.setup: Ryan uses vague bro-language to ask Dwight to position Erin next to him — clearly for romantic reasons
jokes.punchline: Dwight interprets it literally in volleyball terms and offers Phyllis as a superior alternative, completely missing the point; his sincerity makes it work
jokes.explanation: Effective Dwight obliviousness gag. The 'sly dog' line (someone in the crowd catching on before Dwight does) adds a nice layer. Dwight's literal interpretation of social behavior is one of his defining comedic traits and this is a solid execution.

jokes.text: Dwight misreads Ryan's request to be next to Erin as wanting her to set up his spike — 'Sly dog' — then puts him next to Phyllis instead
jokes.setup: Ryan wants to be next to Erin romantically; Dwight thinks it's a volleyball strategy
jokes.punchline: Dwight assumes Ryan wants the tactical advantage of a good setter and rewards him with Phyllis — completely missing the point. 'Sly dog' makes it worse.
jokes.explanation: A good Dwight misunderstanding — he's so focused on the game that he genuinely misses the romantic subtext and accidentally insults Ryan by replacing Erin with Phyllis. 'Sly dog' — approving of a strategy Ryan doesn't intend — is a nice touch.

jokes.text: Holly reveals she and AJ are designing a house together; immediately cut to Michael: 'I'm designing a chair.'
jokes.setup: Holly casually mentions that she and AJ are designing a house together — signaling serious domestic commitment
jokes.punchline: Cut to Michael in confessional, deflated, announcing he too is designing something: a chair. The asymmetry (house vs. chair) encapsulates Michael's position perfectly.
jokes.explanation: This is an exceptional visual/editing joke. The cutting from 'we're designing a house' to Michael's mournful 'I'm designing a chair' is a masterclass in comedic juxtaposition. A house vs. a chair. The implication that Michael has retreated into a small, solitary design project as a response to Holly's settled domestic life is simultaneously funny and sad — the show's signature tonal blend. Economy is nearly perfect: three words convey Michael's entire emotional state.

jokes.text: Michael explains his chair design: 'It's part of your pants. You sit down, you're supported.'
jokes.setup: Michael has announced he is designing a chair
jokes.punchline: The chair is literally just pants with structural support — essentially pants that ARE a chair — which is both absurd and not entirely unlike existing fashion accessories
jokes.explanation: The chair-pants concept is genuinely funny because Michael explains it with such sincerity and the concept is just absurd enough to seem like something someone might have actually dreamed up. 'You sit down, you're supported' as a design brief for what is essentially pants is a funny detail.

jokes.text: Holly remembers Michael's chair pants idea from before, indicating he's been developing this for some time.
jokes.setup: Michael shares his chair-pants concept as if new
jokes.punchline: Holly has heard this before — 'I remember your chair pants idea' — suggesting Michael has been workshopping chair pants as a concept for years
jokes.explanation: The callback deepens the joke: this isn't a new idea Michael had in response to Holly moving on. He's been carrying chair pants as a concept. It also works as a Holly character beat — she knows his quirks fondly. The intimacy between them via shared history of chair pants is genuinely sweet and funny.

jokes.text: Michael puts Holly down for a pair of chair pants, says 'All right, fatty. I will do it.'
jokes.setup: Holly and Michael are riffing warmly on chair pants; Holly asks to be put down for a pair (size 34 waist)
jokes.punchline: Michael responds to a perfectly normal waist size with 'All right, fatty' — a completely unwarranted and disproportionate insult delivered with zero malice, as if it's a friendly nickname
jokes.explanation: Michael's casual 'fatty' is a good cringe joke. The audience would gasp-laugh because it's completely disproportionate to a size 34, and Michael delivers it as pure affection. It's the kind of thing that only works in their specific dynamic and the character integration is high.

jokes.text: 'You guys are really gonna do this?' / 'You bet your fat ass we are.'
jokes.setup: Someone expresses skepticism about Michael and Holly's improv sketch performance
jokes.punchline: 'You bet your fat ass we are' — Michael doubles down on the 'fatty' running gag immediately after using it once
jokes.explanation: The quick callback to 'fat ass' after 'fatty' is a mini running gag — Michael has now committed to fat-shaming for no reason twice in 30 seconds. It gets a laugh for the escalation but is clearly the weaker half of the pair.

jokes.text: Michael and Holly launch into their improv bit: 'Have ya hoyd the news? Extry, extry! Read all about it!'
jokes.setup: Michael announces that the 'old comedy team is back together' and they launch into an improv sketch for the company picnic
jokes.punchline: Their chosen bit is a vaudevillian newsie impression — extremely dated, zero context, and performed with maximum commitment
jokes.explanation: The comedy here is meta — the bit itself is deliberately bad, dated comedy, and the audience's discomfort at watching Michael and Holly do this is where the laugh lives. The vaudevillian newsie impression is a specific choice that signals Michael's comedy sensibility is decades out of date. Decent cringe setup but the payoff is mostly structural rather than joke-based.

jokes.text: Michael as a newsboy approaches a blind man (with sunglasses) and asks 'Are you blind?' then doubles down: 'Sir, with the glasses, are you literally blind? You might be in danger.'
jokes.setup: Michael is doing a newsboy bit and approaches a man with sunglasses who he mistakes for being blind
jokes.punchline: Michael sincerely inquires about the man's blindness as a safety concern; the man reveals they're expensive Ray-Bans and calls him a jackass
jokes.explanation: This is an effective cringe beat. Michael's genuine concern for the possibly-blind man while remaining in character is very Michael — he can't separate performance from reality. The 'You might be in danger' escalation is a good punchline within the bit. The Ray-Bans reveal and 'jackass' dismissal is a satisfying button.

jokes.text: Michael approaches someone wearing expensive sunglasses, asking if they're blind, then doubling down: 'with the glasses, are you literally blind? You might be in danger.'
jokes.setup: Michael is doing a newspaper-boy bit and approaches someone
jokes.punchline: He asks if they're blind — apparently based on the sunglasses — and won't let it go even when it's clearly offensive. 'You might be in danger' — Michael's concern is genuine, which makes it worse.
jokes.explanation: A cringe moment that works through Michael's oblivious persistence. The man's response ('These are expensive Ray-Bans, jackass') is a perfect straight-man reaction.

jokes.text: Kevin barges into the newsboy bit, joining in: 'Are... you... blind? Can you see things with your eyeballs?'
jokes.setup: Michael and Holly are doing a street-level improv; Kevin crashes it
jokes.punchline: Kevin's contribution to the bit — 'Can you see things with your eyeballs?' — is aggressively stupid and unsubtle, embarrassing everyone involved while Kevin is fully committed
jokes.explanation: Kevin asking 'can you see things with your eyeballs?' is peak Kevin — he's so eager to contribute that he strips the inquiry down to its most elemental and dumb phrasing. The character integration is very strong. Michael's exasperated 'Kevin, come on!' while remaining in character adds to it.

jokes.text: Michael addresses the volleyball team: 'You're better than this.' Long pause. 'I am better than this.'
jokes.setup: Michael is giving a team pep talk after the street performance goes badly
jokes.punchline: His encouragement immediately pivots to being about himself: 'I am better than this' — the rallying cry becomes a personal complaint
jokes.explanation: Beautifully structured. The beat between 'you're better than this' and 'I am better than this' is the entirety of Michael's management philosophy compressed into one exchange. He starts with a generic inspiring speech, but it folds back into his narcissism in one sentence. The pause is essential to the joke's architecture. Highly efficient and character-specific.

jokes.text: Ryan sitting on the ground during the game, saying 'We've been out here for a while. I don't need this.'
jokes.setup: Ryan is supposed to be playing in the company volleyball game but is sitting on the ground
jokes.punchline: Ryan's complaint that they've 'been out here a while' and he doesn't 'need this' — as if he has better options and attending a company event is beneath his tolerance level
jokes.explanation: Very Ryan. The entitlement, the disdain, sitting directly on the ground mid-game as if he's above it. 'I don't need this' from someone who clearly needs everything is a good character note. Not the sharpest Ryan joke but solidly character-integrated.

jokes.text: Charles calls a rule violation on Pam's hand touching the net; Dwight objects; Charles insists on taking the point.
jokes.setup: The volleyball game between Scranton and Corporate is very competitive
jokes.punchline: Charles — a VP-level executive — is laser-focused on getting a point via a minor net violation in a corporate picnic volleyball game, revealing that Corporate's petty competitiveness mirrors Scranton's
jokes.explanation: Functional joke about institutional competitiveness bleeding into trivial situations. The comedy is in Charles's seriousness, but it's not particularly sharply written — it relies mostly on context rather than any specific comedic craft.

jokes.text: Pam's confessional revelation: 'Maybe I played a little in junior high. And in high school. Maybe a little in college. And went to volleyball camp most summers.'
jokes.setup: Pam is playing in the volleyball game and suddenly reveals she's much better than expected; Charles accuses her of being a ringer
jokes.punchline: Pam's 'confession' keeps escalating — junior high becomes high school becomes college becomes 'volleyball camp most summers' — each step further undermining her earlier pretense of being an amateur
jokes.explanation: Great structure on this one. The escalation is the joke — each additional qualifier ('in high school,' 'in college,' 'volleyball camp most summers') moves further from casual experience toward serious commitment. The rhythm is excellent. It works because Pam is usually positioned as the low-key normal one, so her hidden athletic depth is an unexpected character reveal played for comedy.

jokes.text: Michael bringing 'snacky snacks' and distributing them during the volleyball timeout
jokes.setup: The volleyball game pauses for a moment
jokes.punchline: Michael refers to snacks as 'snacky snacks' — the infantilizing diminutive is a small but characteristic touch, and the gesture of providing snacks like a team mom is incongruous with his role
jokes.explanation: A minor character beat — 'snacky snacks' is a classically Michael infantilism. Not a strong standalone joke but adds texture. The visual of Michael approaching with snacks like a soccer mom is the real laugh.

jokes.text: Michael reveals he planned to 'wing' the entire Dunder Mifflin history sketch; Holly responds: 'Crystal cool.'
jokes.setup: Holly asks Michael what he has planned for the sketch; he admits he has no script and plans to improvise
jokes.punchline: Holly's 'crystal cool' — a slightly-off slang phrase that reveals she's as awkward as Michael and is trying to match his energy — is both a character beat and a funny verbal tic
jokes.explanation: The 'crystal cool' response is good Holly characterization — she and Michael are kindred spirits in their slightly-off social register. The cringe comes from the mutual blind enthusiasm for what the audience already knows will be a disaster. Good setup for the Slumdunder sequence.

jokes.text: Andy injures himself during volleyball: 'Ow, my ankle!' / 'What happened?' / 'I twisted it.' / 'You weren't even moving.'
jokes.setup: Andy is playing volleyball with great enthusiasm
jokes.punchline: Andy sustains a seemingly significant ankle injury while standing completely still — the injury requiring no movement is the absurdist punchline
jokes.explanation: The kicker — 'you weren't even moving' — is a perfect punchline. Andy injuring himself while stationary is absurd and perfectly in character for him. The four-beat structure (injury claim, question, explanation, disbelief) is tight. Very quotable line.

jokes.text: Rolph refuses to sub in for Pam: 'I don't hear cheaters, tramps, or women who break my friend's heart.'
jokes.setup: Pam is injured and needs a sub; Dwight calls Rolph in to replace her
jokes.punchline: Rolph refuses with an extreme, escalating list of grievances against Pam — 'cheaters, tramps, women who break my friend's heart' — delivered with total conviction as if these are established categories of people he has excommunicated from his hearing
jokes.explanation: A great joke. Rolph has been introduced as a terrifying individual (the shoe store setup, the DEET), and his refusal to sub in because of Pam's romantic history with Dwight is the perfect deployment of that characterization. The phrasing 'I don't hear cheaters, tramps, or women who break my friend's heart' — as if these are established categories of persons he has blocked from his auditory perception — is genuinely original and very funny. The escalating specificity ('women who break my friend's heart' as a distinct category from 'tramps') is excellent.

jokes.text: Michael and Holly brainstorming ideas for the sketch: 'Back to the Future' where they convince 'Dunder and Mifflin to go back in time to fix their parents.' Then 'Jaws': 'Dun-der, Dun-der, Dunder Dunder Dunder...'
jokes.setup: Michael and Holly need a concept for their Dunder Mifflin history sketch and are workshopping ideas
jokes.punchline: Their 'ideas' are just famous movie plots with 'Dunder Mifflin' awkwardly inserted — and they deliver them with full creative confidence, culminating in Michael doing the Jaws theme by chanting 'Dun-der'
jokes.explanation: This is a terrific sketch-comedy-within-the-show moment. The Back to the Future pitch is already funny in its lazy logic ('fix their parents' is a misremembering of the plot), but the Jaws riff elevates it — Michael adapting the 'duh-nuh' shark theme into 'Dun-der' is inspired. Both jokes show Michael's particular brand of confident incompetence as a creative collaborator. Very character-specific.

jokes.text: 'We haven't found our great idea yet.' / 'We're circling it.'
jokes.setup: After a parade of bad ideas, Michael and Holly assess their brainstorm
jokes.punchline: Holly's 'we're circling it' is delivered as genuine confidence about a creative process that has produced nothing
jokes.explanation: Holly's 'we're circling it' is a wonderfully absurd piece of workshop-speak applied to a situation that has produced zero good ideas. It reveals that she and Michael are equally deluded about their creative powers, which is both funny and endearing. Economical and character-specific.

jokes.text: After the volleyball victory, Dwight trash-talks: 'They're gonna wipe their asses with your serves! Piss all over your faces!'
jokes.setup: Scranton advances in the volleyball tournament and Dwight is taunting the next opponents
jokes.punchline: Dwight's trash talk escalates immediately to bodily function imagery — 'wipe their asses with your serves, piss all over your faces' — delivered with athletic seriousness
jokes.explanation: Dwight's trash talk going straight to scatological imagery is an easy but effective character comedy beat. It's broad but it fits. Not especially original or crafted, but the delivery makes it work.

jokes.text: Michael and Holly's sketch title: 'Slumdunder Mifflinaire!'
jokes.setup: Michael and Holly are about to perform their Dunder Mifflin history sketch for the assembled company picnic
jokes.punchline: The sketch is titled 'Slumdunder Mifflinaire' — a portmanteau of 'Slumdog Millionaire' (then-current Best Picture winner) and 'Dunder Mifflinaire' — a reference so timely and so nerdy it's almost charming
jokes.explanation: The title joke works on multiple levels: it's a clever portmanteau, it's timely (Slumdog Millionaire won Best Picture in 2009, the same year this aired), and it perfectly captures Michael's reference-heavy, pun-based comedy style. The word itself is pleasurably absurd to say. For a title gag, it's quite good.

jokes.text: The game-show format of Slumdunder Mifflinaire: asking trivia about Dunder Mifflin's founding as if it's Who Wants to Be a Millionaire
jokes.setup: Michael and Holly have framed Dunder Mifflin company history as a trivia game show, with Holly as contestant
jokes.punchline: The absurdist premise — company founding trivia treated with the gravity and format of a major game show — combined with one of the answer choices always being 'Brushing their teeth' (a non-answer) escalates into ridiculous territory
jokes.explanation: The game show format is a genuinely clever structural choice for a company history presentation. The recurring 'Brushing their teeth' as a nonsense answer option is a running gag within the sketch. As a sustained bit, it's well-constructed even if individual beats vary in quality.

jokes.text: Holly plays both Robert Dunder and Robert Mifflin with a brief moment of announcing herself, then: 'I'm Robert Dunder.' 'I'm Robert Mifflin.' Then Michael as narrator: 'Robert Mifflin had a great life. But unfortunately, had undiagnosed depression, which 9 million Americans suffer from, and is very treatable.'
jokes.setup: The sketch is dramatizing the founding of Dunder Mifflin with Holly playing both founders
jokes.punchline: The PSA-style pivot mid-sketch to flag that depression 'is very treatable' — inserted into what is supposed to be a comedy bit — is extremely Michael: he cannot resist turning a bit into an educational moment
jokes.explanation: The PSA insertion is a great bit: Michael is narrating what is supposed to be a comedy sketch and cannot help adding 'which 9 million Americans suffer from, and is very treatable' as if reading from a brochure. It's completely incongruous with the tone of a game show, which makes it very funny. The joke is also very true to Michael's character — his desire to do good undermines his comedy at every turn.

jokes.text: The sketch reveals Robert Mifflin had 'undiagnosed depression, which 9 million Americans suffer from, and is very treatable.' — mid-comedy sketch PSA
jokes.setup: The comedy sketch is dramatizing the company's history
jokes.punchline: Out of nowhere, the sketch pivots to a PSA about clinical depression — including statistics and the reassurance that it's 'very treatable' — while still framed as entertainment
jokes.explanation: The tonal whiplash of inserting a depression awareness PSA into a company history sketch is genuinely unexpected and funny. '9 million Americans' and 'very treatable' in the middle of What should be comedy is absurdist and dark in equal measure. This is where the sketch starts its slide into disaster — and that's the joke.

jokes.text: The suicide question: 'For $250, how did he kill himself? A) A rope. B) A knife. C) A gun. D) Brushing his teeth!'
jokes.setup: Following the PSA about Robert Mifflin's depression, the game show immediately asks contestants how he committed suicide, with answer choices
jokes.punchline: The casual, game-show framing of a suicide method ('C) A gun. He shot himself... in the head. That is correct!') is bracingly dark for a company picnic; the 'Brushing his teeth' option (a callback to the running gag) provides absurdist relief
jokes.explanation: This is the peak of the Slumdunder sketch's dark comedy. Turning 'how did Mifflin commit suicide?' into a multiple choice question with game-show fanfare is genuinely audacious. The audience reaction ('I usually don't enjoy the theater. But this is delightful.') works as a satirical comment on comedy that succeeds despite being inappropriate. The 'Brushing his teeth' option keeps the absurdist thread alive. Strong joke.

jokes.text: A Dunder Mifflin employee confessional: 'I usually don't enjoy the theater. But this is delightful.'
jokes.setup: The audience is watching Michael and Holly's sketch, which has just revealed a company founder committed suicide via a gun to the head in game show format
jokes.punchline: An audience member finds this 'delightful' — the word 'delightful' for content this dark is the joke
jokes.explanation: The 'I usually don't enjoy the theater' setup is a classic misdirect — you expect a critique, instead you get 'delightful.' The contrast between the content (suicide game show) and the descriptor ('delightful') is the joke. Very economical and well-placed.

jokes.text: The Buffalo closing question: '$500,000 — is it A) Scranton, B) Buffalo, C) Utica, or D) Toothbrush?'
jokes.setup: The sketch reaches its final question about which branch is closing next, with the game-show stakes elevated to $500,000
jokes.punchline: 'D) Toothbrush' — the running gag of the ridiculous wrong answer shifts from 'brushing their teeth' to 'toothbrush,' maintaining the joke while slightly varying it
jokes.explanation: The toothbrush variant is the running gag's third appearance and it's notably weaker than its predecessors — the joke has been well-established by now. The episode earns its score here primarily from setup rather than execution, as the punchline of this joke is actually the Buffalo revelation, not the toothbrush.

jokes.text: Holly answers the Buffalo question correctly because 'David Wallace told me!' — revealing she got the information in confidence and accidentally disclosed a branch closing to the employees at a picnic
jokes.setup: The game show has asked which branch is closing; Holly answers 'Buffalo' with great confidence
jokes.punchline: Her source is David Wallace himself — meaning she accidentally turned confidential corporate intelligence into a game show answer at the company picnic, in front of the Buffalo employees
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's comedic and dramatic peak. The structure is exceptional: the entire Slumdunder sketch has been building toward a punchline that is simultaneously the funniest and most consequential moment in the episode. The use of a game show format to accidentally announce a branch closing — with all the affected employees present — is a brilliant piece of plotting. The moment 'How did you know that?' / 'David Wallace told me!' lands, the comedy and the drama fully merge. This is what The Office does at its best. Among the best-plotted jokes of the series.

jokes.text: David Wallace is confronted publicly: 'David, is this true?' and he hedges: 'OK, we're at a picnic today.'
jokes.setup: Buffalo employees demand confirmation from David Wallace
jokes.punchline: 'OK, we're at a picnic today' — David's absurdly mild contextual redirect ('we're at a picnic!') as his first attempt to manage a branch-closure announcement is corporate-speak comedy at its finest
jokes.explanation: David Wallace's 'we're at a picnic' is a masterclass in corporate deflection — acknowledging the inappropriateness of the venue rather than the content. It's how a CEO tries to buy time after a disaster. The economy of the line is exceptional; it says everything about how management handles bad news.

jokes.text: Buffalo employees protesting: 'We're the best branch in the company!' while David Wallace is forced to make an announcement at a picnic
jokes.setup: The Buffalo closing has just been accidentally revealed through a comedy sketch
jokes.punchline: The absurd escalation — David Wallace having to give a serious layoff announcement at a company picnic because of a comedy sketch — is pure cringe comedy
jokes.explanation: The fallout scene works as sustained cringe. Wallace having to give a somber corporate announcement at a party while surrounded by picnic decorations is an image-based joke that the show trusts the audience to appreciate without underlining. The employees' outrage ('we're the best branch!') adds appropriate chaos.

jokes.text: David Wallace confronts Michael: 'How could you think that the right way to announce a branch closing was in a comedy sketch at the company picnic?'
jokes.setup: Wallace is furious at Michael for revealing the Buffalo closing
jokes.punchline: The question perfectly encapsulates the absurdity of the situation — that it genuinely needs to be said aloud that a comedy sketch is not the proper venue for corporate downsizing announcements
jokes.explanation: The line works as both a straight dramatic moment and a comedic one — the fact that Wallace literally has to say this to an adult man is funny in itself. It also functions as a comedic summary of the entire Slumdunder sequence.

jokes.text: David confronts Michael: 'How could you think that the right way to announce a branch closing was in a comedy sketch at the company picnic?'
jokes.setup: The Buffalo announcement disaster has just played out
jokes.punchline: The question 'How could you think...' is unanswerable — and we know Michael didn't think. The formal phrasing of the question encapsulates Michael's management style being genuinely incomprehensible to a rational person.
jokes.explanation: Works as the rational response to Michael's chaos. Less funny than the disaster itself but necessary as the button.

jokes.text: After being told a small boy said 'Is my daddy gonna have a job by Christmas?', Michael responds: 'He's just thinking about his own gifts.'
jokes.setup: Wallace or someone relays the devastating anecdote of a child worried about their parent's job security
jokes.punchline: Michael dismisses the child's worry as being fundamentally selfish — about presents, not parental employment — completely missing the emotional weight of the situation
jokes.explanation: This is a great Michael Scott line. The joke works by having Michael appear to start empathizing with the child's concern and then completely reframe it in the least empathetic way possible — the child asking about dad's job is actually just worried about Christmas gifts. It's dark, character-perfect, and highly quotable. The structure (apparent empathy → total misreading) is clean. Michael's obliviousness here is at its most precise.

jokes.text: 'A little boy said to me, 'Is my daddy gonna have a job by Christmas?' / 'He's just thinking about his own gifts.'
jokes.setup: David is trying to convey the human cost of the Buffalo announcement to Michael
jokes.punchline: Michael reframes a child's existential fear about their father's employment as self-interested gift anxiety — missing the pathos entirely and landing on the most reductive possible interpretation
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes — possibly the best single line. David Wallace gives Michael an emotionally resonant anecdote about a child fearing for their family's security, and Michael's response ('He's just thinking about his own gifts') is the perfect reduction of that fear to selfishness. It's dark, it's DEEPLY Michael — he genuinely believes this is an insight — and it's a perfect two-sentence exchange. Economy is near-perfect. Earns 8.5+ comfortably.

jokes.text: Dwight's reasoning for still playing volleyball: 'Because if we don't play, then the other team wins.' / 'Dwight's right. Corporate deserves to get its ass kicked.'
jokes.setup: The team debates whether to continue the volleyball game given the Buffalo crisis
jokes.punchline: Dwight's tautological logic ('if we don't play, they win') is accepted by everyone including Jim, who adds the more emotionally satisfying reason: corporate deserves it
jokes.explanation: Dwight's completely circular logic being treated as wisdom is a nice beat, and Jim's addition ('Corporate deserves to get its ass kicked') recontextualizes the game as class warfare, which is simultaneously funny and emotionally satisfying given the Buffalo situation. Good momentum joke.

jokes.text: 'Corporate deserves to get its ass kicked.' — Dwight's justification for continuing the game
jokes.setup: The team discusses whether playing corporate at volleyball is appropriate given the branch closure news
jokes.punchline: Dwight cuts through all sentiment with pure competitive spite — 'Corporate deserves to get its ass kicked' — and somehow this is the most compelling argument anyone makes
jokes.explanation: Eight words of pure Dwight. He doesn't engage with the emotional argument at all — he reframes everything as an adversarial sports contest. And the funny thing is he's not wrong. Economy excellent.

jokes.text: Charles trash-talks from the other side of the net: 'Now it's seven-six. Or is that too much accounting for you?'
jokes.setup: The volleyball game is closely contested; Charles is trash-talking Scranton
jokes.punchline: Charles mocks Scranton as an accounting branch that can't keep track of a simple score — a slightly odd trash-talk given that accounting is a core competency
jokes.explanation: Competent trash-talk joke that leans on Charles's arrogance. The accounting dig is mildly clever — paper company insults typically land around the office work — but it's not particularly sharp. Functional character comedy.

jokes.text: 'Now it's seven-six. Or is that too much accounting for you?'
jokes.setup: The volleyball score is being called out
jokes.punchline: The dig 'is that too much accounting for you?' implies the opponent is bad at math — a white-collar workplace insult at a sporting event
jokes.explanation: Mild office-world sports trash talk. The accounting dig is specific to the work context but not very original. Functional background humor.

jokes.text: Rolph trash-talks Pam: 'Here's an accounting question. What does one fiancee plus one lover equal? Answer: one whore.'
jokes.setup: The volleyball trash-talk is escalating; Rolph continues his hostility toward Pam on Dwight's behalf
jokes.punchline: Rolph frames a vicious personal attack as a math problem — 'accounting question' — making it formally parallel to Charles's previous accounting joke, but going much darker
jokes.explanation: Rolph's math problem is a brilliant structural joke. By framing it as 'an accounting question' (a callback to Charles's previous line), it sets up the expectation of sports trash-talk and then delivers something far more savage and personal. The equation format ('one fiancee plus one lover equals one whore') is both dark and formally clever. The joke tells you everything about Rolph's character — his loyalty to Dwight is total and terrifying, and he will cross any social line in service of it. Very strong.

jokes.text: Jim argues Pam needs to get her ankle examined — 'You're putting a volleyball game in front of your fiancee's health.'
jokes.setup: Pam has twisted her ankle and the opposing team accuses Jim of trying to remove their best player
jokes.punchline: Jim turns their accusation back on them — 'You're putting a volleyball game in front of your fiancee's health' — using concern for Pam as both genuine and tactical
jokes.explanation: A good rhetorical reversal — Jim flips the accusation on his accusers with some justification. His dual motive (protect Pam AND protect the team) makes it a fun ironic moment.

jokes.text: Dwight offers to scout a hospital: 'I spotted a small hospital a few kilometers south of here.'
jokes.setup: Pam has injured her ankle and the team is debating whether she needs medical attention
jokes.punchline: Dwight's casual, advance-scout awareness of nearby medical facilities ('a few kilometers south') implies he had already catalogued emergency resources for the picnic area, which is very Dwight
jokes.explanation: A small but well-observed character beat. Of course Dwight would have pre-identified the nearest hospital before attending a company picnic. The 'kilometers' phrasing is also a nice Dwight touch — he uses metric in a show set in America, suggesting a tactical/military influence on his thinking. Character integration is very high.

jokes.text: Michael and Holly's post-mortem on the sketch: 'There weren't any laughs.' / 'No, it was a tough audience.' / 'We wrote it specifically for this audience.'
jokes.setup: Michael and Holly are debriefing after their sketch accidentally revealed a branch closing and caused a crisis
jokes.punchline: They discuss the sketch purely in terms of comedic performance — 'tough audience' — completely sidestepping that they caused a corporate disaster; Holly's observation that 'we wrote it specifically for this audience' is the kicker
jokes.explanation: A beautifully observed character moment. Michael and Holly processing a catastrophic public gaffe purely through the lens of 'was it a good comedy set?' is peak Michael — his self-perception as a performer insulates him from the reality of consequences. Holly's 'we wrote it specifically for this audience' is particularly sharp: she's right, but she's completely misidentifying why it failed. The joke also works as a character-building beat that explains why Michael and Holly are so compatible — they share this delusional performer's worldview.

jokes.text: 'There weren't any laughs.' / 'No, it was a tough audience.' / 'But we wrote it specifically for this audience.'
jokes.setup: Michael and Holly review whether the sketch worked 'before the Buffalo thing'
jokes.punchline: Holly says it was a 'tough audience' — Michael's rebuttal is that they wrote it specifically for this audience, which is the opposite of a reassurance and makes the failure worse
jokes.explanation: A sharp exchange: Holly uses the 'tough audience' excuse all comedians use, and Michael's correction — 'we wrote it specifically for this audience' — is accidentally devastating. If it was written for them and they didn't laugh, that's worse than a tough-audience excuse. Michael doesn't see this, which is the joke.

jokes.text: 'We have a lot of... good material for next year's sketch.' (long pause)
jokes.setup: Michael and Holly are sitting in quiet reflection after the disastrous sketch
jokes.punchline: Michael's silver lining — that accidentally announcing a branch closing at a picnic is 'good material' for future comedy — represents his unshakeable optimism and comic delusion
jokes.explanation: Michael's decision to immediately begin harvesting the Buffalo disaster as comedic material for next year is a perfect encapsulation of his character. He cannot separate his identity as a performer from any experience. Holly's 'I can't wait' in response — again, sincere — shows their shared delusion. The long pause before 'good material' gives the joke its proper weight.

jokes.text: Jim on the phone from the hospital, telling Dwight to stall the volleyball game; Dwight is asked to 'think of something'
jokes.setup: Pam is getting her ankle X-rayed; Jim is calling in to manage the volleyball situation remotely
jokes.punchline: Dwight is left to 'stall' an ongoing competitive volleyball game — an inherently absurd task — and the implication is that whatever he does will be extreme
jokes.explanation: The setup is good — putting Dwight in charge of stalling a volleyball game — but the joke is more of a structural beat than a completed gag. Its punchline lives in what Dwight presumably does next (not shown), making this feel like an unresolved setup.

jokes.text: Doctor doing Pam's X-ray asks: 'No metal plates? No chances you're pregnant?' Then: 'Could we hurry this up? I've got a game to get back to.' / Doctor: 'Good, because my next question was: do you have a game to get back to?'
jokes.setup: A doctor is running through standard pre-X-ray questions
jokes.punchline: The doctor's final 'question' — 'do you have a game to get back to?' — revealed as literally his next standard question, implies the doctor is equally invested in the picnic game and finds the question clinically relevant
jokes.explanation: A very well-constructed joke. The setup is the standard medical intake procedure; when Pam jumps in asking to hurry because of the game, the doctor reveals it was already on his checklist — treating 'do you have a game to get back to?' as clinical information. The absurdist logic that game-urgency is a standard medical consideration is nicely played. Good economy and structure.

jokes.text: Michael tells Holly: 'You guys should hit the road before... I close down another branch.'
jokes.setup: Michael is saying goodbye to Holly and AJ at the end of the day
jokes.punchline: Michael jokes about his own capacity for corporate destruction with a self-aware quip — 'before I close down another branch' — which is unusually self-aware for him
jokes.explanation: Michael being briefly self-aware is a nice character grace note. The line is a callback to the day's disaster and works as both a joke and a moment of genuine connection between him and Holly. The economy is good — it's a lot of information in eight words. Unusual moment of self-deprecation from Michael that feels earned.

jokes.text: Dwight's escalating argument for not forfeiting the game by listing injured people: 'How many people need to get hurt before we learn a valuable lesson? One? Two? Three? Four?' (Jim cuts in repeatedly, Dwight ignores him): 'Five? Six? Seven? Can I finish, please? Eight?'
jokes.setup: The team is debating whether to forfeit the volleyball game since Pam is at the hospital and they need subs
jokes.punchline: Dwight's rhetorical question about injury thresholds ('how many people need to get hurt?') is supposed to argue AGAINST playing, but he keeps going past any sensible stopping point while Jim tries to interject, reaching eight hypothetical casualties with total sincerity
jokes.explanation: This is one of the episode's best extended comedy bits. Dwight's rhetorical escalation is the joke — by the time he reaches eight hypothetical injury victims, the number itself has become the comedy. Jim's constant interruptions while Dwight plows forward is a great double act. The 'Can I finish, please?' at around seven is perfect Dwight — he's so committed to his rhetorical structure that Jim's reasonable objections are an imposition. Very character-specific and well-paced.

jokes.text: Dwight's stalling tactic: 'How many people need to get hurt before we learn a valuable lesson? One? Two? Three? Four? No, hear me out. Five? Six? Seven? Can I finish, please? Eight?'
jokes.setup: Dwight has been asked to stall the opposing team while Jim and Pam are at the hospital
jokes.punchline: Dwight's stalling consists of asking a rhetorical question and then counting upward with dramatic pauses, getting interrupted, insisting on continuing, and reaching 'eight' — with no answer ever coming
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's standout comedy moments. Dwight's stalling technique — asking a rhetorical question and then slowly counting possible numbers of injured people while being interrupted — is absurdist escalation at its best. 'No, hear me out' and 'Can I finish, please?' as parenthetical defenses while counting to eight is deeply Dwight: he treats every activity with the gravity of high-stakes negotiation. The bit ends at 'eight' with no resolution, which is perfect. Earns 8+ clearly — it's original, structurally excellent, and only Dwight could do this.

jokes.text: Final scene: 'Send in the subs.' — Jim concedes the volleyball game, implying the news from the hospital is significant (Pam is pregnant)
jokes.setup: Throughout the episode Jim has been desperately stalling the volleyball game to wait for Pam to return from the hospital
jokes.punchline: Jim's 'send in the subs' — a quiet concession — signals something has changed at the hospital. The comedy of the elaborate volleyball stalling is retroactively reframed as covering for what will be revealed as a pregnancy announcement. The joke is the misdirection: we thought it was about volleyball.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's emotional and structural peak. Four words — 'send in the subs' — communicate an entire emotional shift. The rewatch bonus is enormous: knowing this concedes the game because Jim and Pam have just learned about the pregnancy makes every previous volleyball-stalling beat retroactively funnier and more poignant. The joke works because of everything that preceded it. Economy is near-perfect: maximum meaning per word. The comedy and the heart of the show are inseparable here, which is The Office at its best.

jokes.text: 'Send in the subs.' — After a long wait, Dwight quietly gives up the stall
jokes.setup: Dwight has been heroically stalling for Jim and Pam; the wait has become unsustainable
jokes.punchline: 'Send in the subs' — said quietly, with resignation, is the anti-climax to all of Dwight's stalling drama. The deflation from 'How many people need to get hurt' to 'send in the subs' is the comedic arc of the episode's final act.
jokes.explanation: Four words as the perfect button to Dwight's entire stalling arc. The shift from dramatic oration to quiet capitulation is the Dwight comedy beat at its most efficient. Economy gets a 10 — four syllables closing an extended comedic sequence.

tmdb_overview: At the company picnic, Michael and Holly are reunited for the first time since their split. The rest of the staff competes in games, such as the volleyball tournament.
